name: Natto gum
lead: Natto gum is a cosmetic ingredient described as a sticky, water-soluble polymer produced by Bacillus bacteria during fermentation of soybeans, as in the Japanese food natto. It is associated with poly-gamma-glutamic acid (gamma-PGA), a water-soluble biodegradable polymer made from glutamic acid.[1][2] In skincare it is listed as a moisturising and film-forming ingredient, used so that the skin surface feels hydrated and looks smoother after a face pack or cream.[3][4]

Natto itself is made by fermenting whole soybeans with Bacillus subtilis var. natto, and its slimy, string-forming coating is a product of that fermentation.[1] Wikipedia's polyglutamic acid article calls gamma-PGA non-immunogenic and biodegradable and classes it as a cosmeceutical, while noting that the page offers no details on its skin effects.[2]

Published sources on natto gum under that name are mostly patents that list it in face packs and creams. No human clinical study of natto gum itself was located. Laboratory work on its closely related polymer, poly-gamma-glutamic acid, includes a 2025 study of keratinocytes and a reconstructed skin model [5].
infobox: 0.5 to 1.5 percent in one face pack[3]

paras: Natto is made by fermenting whole soybeans with Bacillus subtilis var. natto, and its stringy texture is characteristic.[1] Poly-gamma-glutamic acid is a negatively charged, water-soluble polymer produced industrially by Bacillus fermentation; Wikipedia lists it among cosmeceutical uses and describes it as biodegradable and non-immunogenic.[2] The link between natto gum and gamma-PGA is made in ingredient literature rather than in the two Wikipedia pages loaded here, and the exact composition of commercial natto gum was not established from these sources.

Polyglutamic acid exists as gamma-PGA, in which the peptide bond forms through the side-chain carboxyl, and alpha-PGA, formed through the main-chain carboxyl; both are water-soluble and negatively charged.[2] Gamma-PGA is made industrially by bacterial fermentation, and the best-known source is natto, though other Bacillus species produce it as well.[2] Alpha-PGA is manufactured by chemical ring-opening polymerisation.[2] Beyond cosmetics, PGA is studied as a drug-delivery aid, with alpha-PGA used as a carrier for the anticancer drug paclitaxel in paclitaxel poliglumex, and as a water-treatment flocculant.[2]

Natto is eaten at breakfast over rice, often with karashi mustard or soy sauce, and is most popular in eastern Japan.[1] Its origin is uncertain: legends credit samurai Minamoto no Yoshiie, whose troops are said to have fermented boiled soybeans in straw bags during a campaign in 1086-1088, or Prince Shotoku, while a more evidence-based theory links it to Chinese douchi.[1] In the Taisho period (1912-1926) researchers developed a B. subtilis starter culture that no longer required rice straw.[1]

Production involves soaking beans for 12 to 20 hours, steaming them, mixing in the starter and fermenting at about 40 degrees Celsius for up to 24 hours, then cooling to develop stringiness.[1] Glutamic acid develops during fermentation and gives natto its umami flavour, and the stringy mucilage is compared in texture to okra.[1]

A Chinese patent (2008) describes a multifunctional face pack containing nano colloidal silver at 0.0005 to 0.0015 percent, aloe extract at 4 to 8 percent, natto gum at about 0.5 to 1.5 percent, and ginkgo, green tea and lavender extracts.[3] A Korean patent (2009) describes a high-moisturising composition combining cellulose gum, natto gum or hyaluronic acid polymer with a phenyl-modified methicone to form a moisturising membrane, noting the natto gum is obtained by culturing a Bacillus.[4] These are formulation descriptions, not efficacy data.

A 2025 study in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences isolated a Bacillus subtilis strain, HB-31, from a wetland on Jeju Island, Korea, whose mucus-like secretion was identified as high-molecular-weight poly-gamma-glutamic acid [5]. In cultured keratinocytes, the polymer increased expression of skin-barrier and lipid-synthesis genes in a dose-dependent way, along with hyaluronic acid synthase genes and aquaporin 3, a water-channel protein linked to skin hydration [5].

In a reconstructed skin model, a 1 percent topical application raised expression of filaggrin, involucrin, CD44 and aquaporin 3 compared with an untreated control [5]. The authors suggest the strain could be a production platform for gamma-PGA that may help the skin barrier and moisture retention, and note that long-term effects need further study [5]. This work concerns gamma-PGA in cell and tissue models rather than a product labelled natto gum, and it is not a human trial.

No safety data on natto gum in skincare were found. Natto as a food provides vitamin K, including the menaquinones MK-7 and MK-8, which can counteract the anticoagulant warfarin, so people on that drug are advised to keep intake consistent; this concerns eating natto rather than topical use.[1]

No studies found on natto gum in skin. Related laboratory work on poly-gamma-glutamic acid in keratinocytes and a reconstructed skin model is described above [5]; other literature describes gamma-PGA and natto in terms of chemistry and manufacturing rather than skin outcomes [2][1].

card.summary: A fermented-soybean polymer used as a humectant in face packs; documented in patents, not in trials.

quick.overview:
Natto gum is a sticky polymer from Bacillus fermentation of soybeans, listed in some face packs and moisturisers.
It appears in patents as a moisturising ingredient; no human study was found.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a water-binding, film-forming polymer that holds moisture on the skin, related to poly-gamma-glutamic acid.
quick.risks: No safety data are available. Soy-derived ingredients can be an allergen for some people.

chain: Sticky polymer binds water and forms a film on the skin
Skin looks plumper and more even while hydrated
angle.text: Natto gum is listed in face packs and moisturisers as a water-holding, film-forming ingredient. People use products containing it for hydrated, smoother-looking skin, and the evidence base consists of formulation patents rather than trials.
